studies.title: Arise And Warn
studies.meaning: Five imperatives in a row, each shorter than an English sentence, and the order matters. Stand up; warn; declare your Lord greater; clean your clothes; keep away from what defiles. Commentators divide over the fourth. Some read the clothes literally, as the plain cleanliness of a man who is about to stand in front of a town, others as a known Arabic figure in which a person's garment stands for his conduct. Most record both readings side by side rather than choosing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and by most accounts among the very earliest passages, arriving soon after the first revelation. The sources describe the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) covered in a cloak when it came and read the opening address literally. The instruction to rise and warn marks the moment a private experience became a public office. From here the mission had an audience, and Mecca had a problem to solve.

keyTerms.note: A participle for somebody who has drawn a covering over himself. The form is reflexive, so the word names something he has done rather than a station he holds, and the instruction is to come out from under it.
The verb makes something great by saying so rather than by adding to it. The noun formed from it is the name Arabic gives to the formula that opens every prayer.

A word whose root covers filth and also the punishment that follows it. Commentators read it as the idols, as wrongdoing in general, or as anything that soils, and they record the range without deciding.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Clothes were few and expensive. A man might own two garments, wash them at a well, and wear the same wool through a whole season, so a stained robe was a visible fact that everyone in a small town could read. Men attached to the sanctuary paid attention to appearance because they were constantly watched. An instruction about a garment, given to a man about to stand up in front of Mecca, was practical before it was anything else.
studies.didYouKnow: Two neighbouring surahs open by addressing the same man in the same posture, using two words built on different roots that mean almost exactly the same thing: one for wrapping yourself up, one for covering yourself over. They sit side by side in the Quran's order. The instruction after each is different: one asks for a night of standing, the other for a day of speaking.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The commissioning arrives as a list of actions with no explanation attached, and that is itself a claim about what prophecy is. There is no argument offered to be convinced by and no vision described; there is a man told to get up. The pairing of an outward instruction about clothing with an inward one about defilement sets a pattern the Quran keeps throughout: the visible and the hidden addressed in the same breath, at the same level of seriousness.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same man in the same posture and asks for a night practice instead of a public one.
Gives the same instruction to warn, beginning with the nearest relatives and widening outward.
Tells him to come out into the open with what he has been commanded to carry.

studies.applyIt: The second word of this passage is stand. Whatever you have been meaning to say to somebody and keep putting off, a warning, a worry, an apology, do the physical part today. Get up, find them, be in the room. The passage separates rising from speaking, and the rising is the part most of us never reach.

studies.title: Give Without Counting It
studies.meaning: The first instruction is the hardest to render and the commentators give a spread: do not give in order to receive more, do not treat your own effort as a favour done to God, do not regard what you deliver as large. What the readings share is a warning against the arithmetic of exchange entering the work at all. Then the scene jumps without transition. A trumpet sounds, and the day is named twice, once as hard and once as not easy, with the second phrase narrowed to those who refused.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the commissioning that opens the surah. The warning against seeking a return belongs to a setting where patronage was how anything at all got done: gifts created obligations, and obligations were called in publicly. The community was small and the mission had nothing funding it, so the instruction bears on its own economics before it bears on anything general.

keyTerms.note: The verb means both to give and to remind the recipient that you gave. Arabic uses one word for the gift and for the debt it creates, which is exactly the confusion the instruction closes off.
A form that means asking for a lot and also regarding something as a lot. Both senses are attested here, and both describe somebody keeping a running total of what he has put in.
An instrument named from a verb for striking or boring through. The word occurs once in the Quran; every other passage naming the same signal uses an entirely different term.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gifts in Arabia were instruments, not gestures. A chief gave camels and the receiving man's obligation became public and was remembered; poets recited who had given what, and a favour unrepaid stood as a claim for years. Nothing moved without this system, and there was no courteous way to step outside it. Telling a man beginning a public mission not to give with any expectation of return removed the only currency he had.
studies.didYouKnow: The trumpet named in the third of these ayat occurs once in the entire Quran. Every other passage describing the same signal reaches for a different word, one used more than ten times. This single occurrence sits in one of the earliest surahs, built on a verb that means to strike a thing until it sounds.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two instructions about interior accounting are set immediately beside the sounding of a trumpet, and the juxtaposition is the argument. A person who keeps score of what he has given is treating this life as the place where the books get balanced. The trumpet says they are balanced elsewhere. The closing line is then careful in a way that is easy to miss: it calls the day hard, and withholds the word easy only from those who refused.

crossReferences.why: Describes giving undone by reminders of the favour, the posture this passage warns against in advance.
Has the righteous say plainly that they want no reward and no thanks from those they fed.
Describes the single blast of the trumpet and the day it opens, in the same early register.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you did for somebody in the past month that you have mentioned since, either to them or to a third person. Notice the small pleasure in the mentioning. This week, do one thing that nobody will ever hear about from you, and let the silence around it be the whole point rather than a sacrifice.

studies.title: I Made His Road Smooth
studies.meaning: One man is drawn in five short strokes, and every stroke but the last is something handed to him. He arrived with nothing; wealth was stretched out for him; sons stood beside him in the town; his road was levelled in advance. Then the movement reverses in the final line, where he is found expecting more. Classical reports identify the man from the circumstances of the surah, and the commentators treat the description rather than the identification as the thing being offered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The opposition to the mission was led by men of substantial wealth whose position rested on the existing arrangement of the sanctuary and the trade that ran through it. The classical sources attach this passage to one such figure and read the ayat that follow as his considered public response to hearing the recitation. The reports agree on the outline of the episode and differ over its details.

keyTerms.note: Read two ways by the commentators: that God alone created him, or that he came into the world singly with nothing. Either reading sets up the list of gifts that follows, none of which he brought with him.
A participle from the verb to stretch. Wealth is described as something pulled out lengthwise, like cloth off a bolt, which carries duration and continuity rather than the image of a heap.
The word for witnesses, used of sons who are at hand rather than away trading. Grown sons in the town were the visible form of standing, which makes them part of his public credit.
From the root that gives the word for a cradle and for flattened ground. It pictures a life with the obstacles taken out ahead of time, prepared the way a bed is prepared for somebody.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in Mecca was counted in sons and in camels, and both had to be visible. A man whose boys were grown and in town could press a claim, host a delegation, and know exactly who would stand behind him in a dispute. Wealth merely stored did not register at all; wealth that moved, in feasts and loans and bride-gifts, did. This description is a Meccan inventory of a successful life, taken item by item.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for smoothing a road in the fourth of these ayat shares its root with the Arabic word for a cradle, and the Quran uses that same root for the earth being laid out as a resting place for people. One root covers the flattening of ground, the bed of an infant, and the quiet arrangement of a comfortable life.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage counts a man's blessings back to him as evidence rather than withdrawing them as a punishment. Each item is stated with a first-person verb, so the giving is acknowledged before the complaint is made. What is objected to is not the size of what he has but the direction of his expectation: given everything, he is found still asking. That makes ingratitude a matter of orientation rather than of quantity, which is why the portrait works on readers who own nothing like his wealth.

crossReferences.why: States the mechanism in two lines: a person overreaches the moment he sees himself as self-sufficient.
Describes a man counting his wealth over and imagining it will make him last.
Turns the same figure into a parable: two gardens, sons at hand, and certainty that none of it ends.

studies.applyIt: List four things you did not earn and would not have if the arrangement had been slightly different: where you were born, who taught you to read, a body that works, somebody who stayed. Write them as four lines in the past tense with no commentary attached. This passage is built out of exactly that list, and the man in it had never once made one.

studies.title: How He Calculated
studies.meaning: The passage refuses the expectation raised a line earlier and then names what is actually happening. The word chosen is not disbelief but obstinacy, a settled resistance aimed at signs he could evidently read. What follows is the unusual part. Two ayat describe him thinking and measuring, and then the identical phrase is repeated in the next ayah with a single particle added. The repetition carries no new content. It reproduces the experience of watching somebody deliberate toward a conclusion already chosen.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early, during the season when pilgrims gathered at the fairs around Mecca and the town's leadership needed a line to give visitors about the man reciting in their valley. The classical reports describe the deliberation in these ayat as exactly that: a formula being worked out for public use. The reports name a figure and differ over who else was in the room.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form for one who swerves aside and then holds his ground. It describes a posture rather than an opinion, which is why the passage treats his conclusion as settled before any reasoning begins.
The noun names a climb. Paired with a verb meaning to burden, it pictures a man made to labour up a slope that never levels off, which answers the smoothed road described a few ayat earlier.

From the root for measuring out, which also gives the word for what God determines. Used of a man it means working a thing out to size, and the repetition quietly sets the two uses against each other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The fairs around Mecca were a marketplace for reputation as much as for goods. Poets competed in public, verdicts on verse travelled home with the pilgrims, and a phrase that stuck could finish a man's standing for a generation. Meccan leaders had a practical problem every season: what to tell arrivals about the recitation they were certain to hear. Getting the wording right mattered commercially. These ayat describe a committee choosing a slogan.
studies.didYouKnow: Two consecutive ayat here are word for word identical except for one opening particle, and the repeated wording is a curse. The Quran very rarely repeats a line immediately, and the effect is closer to a pulse than to emphasis: the same words, then the same words again, while nothing in the scene has moved forward at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The failure is located in the will rather than in the intellect. He is shown thinking, and thinking carefully, and the verdict falls on the thinking itself. That is a claim the Quran makes in several places: that reasoning follows a prior orientation, and that careful analysis can be the instrument of refusal rather than its opposite. It leaves the reader unable to treat being persuaded as a purely cognitive event.

crossReferences.why: Says they rejected the signs while their own souls were convinced of them.
Describes men who listen closely and argue afterwards, hearing without anything being received.
Describes a man who takes his own desire as his god and is then sealed inside it.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you are building a case. There is a particular feeling to reasoning toward a conclusion you have already picked: quicker, more fluent, more satisfying than actual thinking. Catch it once this week, and when you do, state the opposing case out loud. Not to adopt it. Only to find out whether you can put it fairly.

studies.title: Then He Frowned And Scowled
studies.meaning: Six verbs across five very short ayat, each introduced by the same connective, so the passage moves like a sequence of stills. He looked; his face closed; he scowled; he turned his back; he swelled. Only then does he speak, and what he produces is a verdict in two halves that undercut each other: inherited magic, and ordinary human speech. Commentators note that the physical description comes first and runs longer than the statement, which reverses the way such a scene would normally be told.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. These ayat continue the account of a leading opponent arriving at a public description of the recitation. The charge he settles on, that it was sorcery handed down from somewhere, was the line Mecca used for years afterwards, and the surrounding surahs answer it repeatedly. The classical reports describe the deliberation in some detail and differ over who was present for it.

keyTerms.note: Two near-synonyms with almost the same consonants. The second adds hostility to the first, moving in one breath from a face that has closed to a face that has turned actively sour.
The reflexive of making great: to make yourself large. It is the same verb used of the refusal to bow before Adam, which fixes its sense as a posture rather than as a considered position.
From the root for a trace or a footprint left behind. Calling the recitation inherited magic puts it in the past, which was the most damaging thing available to say about something claimed to be new.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Faces were read closely and described publicly in that culture; the poetry is full of the exact expressions of men receiving news they did not want. A leader who scowled in front of witnesses had already made a statement before opening his mouth. And the accusation of sorcery was not a vague insult. It named a recognised trade with practitioners across the peninsula, and it told listeners which shelf to put the recitation on.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs describing the man's face differ by a single consonant and share the same rhythm, a sound pairing Arabic uses to make an action feel doubled. One of the two supplies the opening word and the name of a later surah of the Quran, which begins with a frown of an entirely different kind and rebukes it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Arrogance is presented as a bodily event before it is a claim. The turning away and the swelling are described first, and only afterwards the sentence he produces, which makes the verdict a symptom of the posture rather than its cause. That inverts the way people usually account for their own refusals. It also means the passage can be read by somebody who has never denied anything in words, since the sequence it describes begins with a face.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the same verb for frowning, in an entirely different situation, and answers it differently.
Shows the same self-magnifying refusal at the opening of the human story.
Records the same charge from the same quarter: is this anything but a mortal like you.

studies.applyIt: Watch your own face this week during a disagreement. Before you have said a word, something has usually already happened around your mouth and eyes, and the other person has read it accurately. Catch that moment once, and hold your expression open three seconds longer than is comfortable. The sequence in this passage starts precisely there.

studies.title: What Will Convey To You
studies.meaning: A name is given and then immediately declared beyond the hearer's grasp, a formula the Quran uses when it wants a word to stay strange. Two clauses describe it without picturing anything: it leaves nothing and it lets nothing off. Then a figure, nineteen, with no noun attached to it and no explanation. The following ayah supplies part of an answer, but as these five lines stand the number is left bare, and the classical commentators read that bareness as deliberate.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early, and the passage became a matter of public argument in the town almost at once. The reports describe Meccans seizing on the number and making jokes about it, and the next ayah of the same surah addresses that reaction directly, saying the figure was made a trial. The sequence is unusual: a revelation, a mocking response in the streets, and a further revelation answering the response.

keyTerms.note: A name rather than a description. Arabic lexicographers connect it to a verb for the sun scorching and altering a face. The Quran uses it in four places and never once explains it.
Two verbs of leaving something behind, negated together. Arabic pairs them for totality, the way English says nothing whatsoever, so the phrase names an absence of exception rather than an intensity.
An intensive form from a root covering both appearing and changing colour under heat. Commentators read it as burning the skin dark, and the word occurs once in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fire in Mecca was domestic and known by its work: charring, drying, blackening skin. Branding irons marked camels, cooking fires blackened pots, and the sun itself altered a face over the course of a season. The vocabulary here draws entirely on that ordinary experience rather than on anything exotic. What makes it frightening is the two negations, which take away the one thing every fire eventually does, which is to go out and leave something behind.
studies.didYouKnow: The number in the last line provoked immediate public argument in Mecca, and the very next ayah of the same surah answers the reaction to it. The Quran preserves both halves: the statement that drew the mockery, and the response to the mockery, one directly after the other, so a reader today receives the exchange in the order it actually happened.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage works by withholding. A name declared beyond explanation, descriptions that are entirely negative, and a number with nothing attached. The effect is to make the reader conscious of the limit of what is being given rather than to build a picture. That is consistent with how the Quran handles the unseen throughout: enough to be taken seriously, never enough to be imagined comfortably, and the gap is left open deliberately.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same name in another surah, again with no description of what it is.
Uses the identical withholding formula: a name, then what will convey to you what it is.
Names another fire and again asks the reader what could possibly convey it.

studies.applyIt: Notice how hard this passage works at not describing. Pick one thing you habitually explain away, a fear, a grief, a debt you owe somebody, and spend a minute today not explaining it to yourself. Name it and stop there. The discomfort of leaving something unresolved is exactly what these five lines are built to produce.

studies.title: The Number Made A Trial
studies.meaning: The ayah answers a reaction rather than continuing a description, and it works in layers. First it states what the wardens are, and it is not what the objectors were picturing. Then it says the number itself was made a testing, and lists four effects on four groups, so one fact produces certainty in some, an increase in others, an absence of doubt in a third and a question in a fourth. The closing clauses pull back twice: the forces are known only to God, and all of this is a reminder.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early, and unusually this ayah responds to something that had already happened in the town. The reports describe Meccans seizing on the figure given three ayat before and joking about it, one of them offering to deal with the wardens himself. The reference to those given the Scripture points beyond Mecca, to communities in the peninsula whose reaction the ayah expects to be different.

keyTerms.note: The word covers both an ordeal and the assaying of metal in fire to find out what it is. The number does not produce belief or refusal here. It exposes which of the two was already present.
An intensive reflexive of the verb to be sure, so the sense is seeking certainty and arriving at it rather than simply possessing it. It names an outcome that has to be travelled to.
A military word for organised companies. Applying it to what stands over the fire makes the wardens a detachment of something larger rather than a fixed quantity a person could reason his way around.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Numbers carried weight in that world because almost all reckoning was done aloud and held in memory. A tribe's strength, a debt's size, the stages of a journey: these circulated as figures that people repeated, compared and tested against each other. A precise and unexplained number dropped into a warning was therefore something an audience would pick up immediately, turn over and argue about, which is what the reports say happened within days.
studies.didYouKnow: This is by a wide margin the longest ayah in a surah otherwise built from very short ones, several of them only two or three words. The change in length is doing work. The clipped rhythm that carries the whole chapter opens out into one extended paragraph at exactly the point where a public objection has to be met.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah has one piece of information do opposite things to different hearers, and says so explicitly. That is a claim about revelation itself: it does not act uniformly, because what it meets in a person is not uniform. Guiding and leaving astray are then attributed to God in a single clause, and immediately afterwards the whole thing is called a reminder for human beings, which keeps responsibility inside the room.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same point about a small detail: many are guided by it and many led astray.
Says the revelation is healing for believers and increases only loss for the wrongdoers.
Describes a single surah increasing faith in some hearers and defilement in others.

studies.applyIt: Think of a piece of news that landed differently on two people you know. The same fact, opposite reactions, and both of them certain the fact spoke for itself. Notice that you were one of the two. This ayah says the information was never the variable in that exchange. What it met was.

studies.title: The Night As It Withdraws
studies.meaning: Three oaths, then the thing sworn to, which arrives as a pronoun with no clear antecedent. Commentators take it as the fire named a few ayat earlier, or as the surah, or as the warning itself, and the range is left open. What the three oaths share is a turning point: a moon that waxes and wanes, a night caught at the moment it turns its back, a morning caught at the moment it opens out. Each names a threshold rather than a state, which is what the thing sworn to also is.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The surah has just answered a public objection at unusual length, and here it changes register completely, from an extended paragraph of argument into a run of two-word lines. Oath formulas of this shape were the opening move of both Arabian sooth-speech and poetry, so the audience recognised the form immediately, even as what followed refused to behave like either one.

keyTerms.note: A verb used of a person walking away, applied here to the night. The same verb described a man turning his back on the recitation eleven ayat earlier, so refusal and a movement of the sky share one word.
From a root for lifting a covering off a face. The morning is described as unveiling rather than arriving, which makes daylight a matter of something being removed rather than something being added.

A plural of the elative for greatest, standing with no noun attached. Arabic can leave the noun out when the category is meant to stay open, and the commentators accordingly differ over what is being ranked.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The moon governed the calendar, the markets and the pilgrimage seasons, and its phases were watched by everybody rather than by specialists. Night travel was normal because the days were too hot to move in, so the turning of the night was a practical moment: the hour a caravan began looking for somewhere to stop. And the first paling of the sky was when a watchman could finally tell a white thread from a black one.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used of the night turning its back is the same verb used, eleven ayat earlier in this surah, of a man turning his back on what he had heard. The chapter puts a human refusal and a movement of the sky into one word, and the two uses arrive close enough together that anybody hearing the surah through will catch the echo.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Oaths in the Quran are not offered as proofs. They direct attention. Sworn by things everybody has seen, they make an audience look hard at what they take for granted just before a claim is made about what they have not seen. The three chosen here are all thresholds, so the passage argues by shape rather than by evidence: the world you already know is made of turnings, and one more is coming.

crossReferences.why: Swears by the night as it departs and the morning as it breathes, in almost these terms.
Pairs the brightness of morning with a settled night as the opening oath of a short surah.
Runs a comparable sequence of oaths by dawn, by nights, and by night as it passes.

studies.applyIt: Be awake for one turning this week: the last dark before the sky pales, or the moment the light finally goes. Do not do anything with it, and do not photograph it. The oaths in this passage rest on people having noticed these moments, and most of us have arranged our days so that we never do.

studies.title: Every Soul Held In Pledge
studies.meaning: A choice is stated with unusual neutrality: whoever wishes to go forward or to hold back. Then a commercial image, and it is severe. Every soul is a pledge held against what it earned, like an object left with a lender until the debt is settled. One group is exempted, and the passage does not describe their reward at length; it shows them in gardens, asking questions, and the question they ask is about other people.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from an early surah that begins with an instruction to rise and warn. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. They follow a run of oaths by the night, the moon and the morning, and precede a dialogue in which the people of the fire are asked what brought them there. Mecca ran on credit and pledges, so the image would have been immediately familiar.

keyTerms.note: The object a borrower leaves with a lender until the loan is repaid. The soul is not compared to a debtor but to the collateral, which cannot free itself and is held by someone else.
A verb of stepping ahead, paired with its opposite in the same line. The choice is offered without pressure in the sentence itself, which the classical readers note as a deliberate restraint.
A reciprocal form, so the asking goes back and forth. The Arabic makes the scene a conversation rather than an interrogation, and the object of their curiosity is placed in the next line.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Pledging was how business worked without banks. A man borrowing against a harvest left something with the lender, a weapon, a coat of mail, an animal, and it stayed there until he paid. The pledged item was in a strange condition, still his and not available to him. Everyone in Mecca had either held one or handed one over, and knew the specific unease of the arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: The question these people ask gets an answer four ayat later, in the words of those being asked. They name four things: they did not pray, they did not feed the destitute, they talked idly with those who talked idly, and they denied the day of reckoning. It is one of the few places where the Quran lets the condemned give their own account.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together that usually pull apart. The choice to advance or to hold back is left genuinely open in one line, and in the next every soul is described as held as security for what it has done. Freedom and liability are stated side by side without either being softened. The image of a pledge also implies redemption: collateral is held against a debt, which means it is the kind of thing that can be released.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the reply to the question being asked here, four failures named by the people themselves.
Repeats the same image in almost identical words, in a passage about families reunited.
States the same open choice, and follows it immediately with what each choice leads to.

studies.applyIt: The image here is collateral: something of yours held until an account is settled. Pick one actual account you have left open, a debt, an unreturned item, a promise, and settle it this week. Not because it is the same thing. Because the feeling of getting something back is worth having in mind when you read this ayah again.

studies.title: We Did Not Feed Them
studies.meaning: A question is put and the answer comes from the condemned themselves, which is rare. They give four items, and the order repays attention: two omissions, then a habit, then a denial. Prayer and feeding come first, ahead of the belief that would seem to underlie them, and the third item is not an act at all but a way of talking, joining in with people who talk emptily about what they have not examined. The list ends where an accusation would normally begin.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The pairing of prayer with feeding the destitute recurs throughout the earliest surahs, addressed to an audience whose religion was extensive and whose treatment of the poor was not. The exchange is set after the fact and the speakers are not identified, so it works as a category rather than as a case against named people. No occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A verb for passing something through a narrow way, used of a road and of a thread through a needle. It makes the question about the route taken rather than about a verdict handed down.
From a root for stillness. It names somebody whom poverty has brought to a standstill, and Arabic keeps it distinct from the word for a poor man who is still moving and still asking.
The verb for walking into water without knowing its depth. Applied to speech it means talking into subjects you have never sounded, and the Quran treats that as a habit with consequences.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feeding was the visible form of virtue in Arabia and it was competitive. Chiefs were praised in verse for the number of pots they kept over the fire through a hard winter, and hospitality claims were part of a man's standing for years afterwards. What this passage names is not a failure of generosity in general. It is the failure to feed the one person who could never return the meal, which the poetry rarely bothered to celebrate.
studies.didYouKnow: The third item on this list is a way of speaking rather than a deed, and the verb behind it means to wade into water of unknown depth. The Quran uses that image for talking about God and the unseen without knowledge. The speakers name it in the same breath as neglecting prayer and neglecting the poor, as though it belonged in the same order of seriousness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The self-accusation puts practice before creed, reversing the order most people would expect. Prayer and feeding come first and the denial of the Day comes last, so belief is presented as what sits at the bottom of a stack rather than at the top of it. The passage also declines to have anybody else describe them. The record is given in their own words, which settles any question of its accuracy.

crossReferences.why: Ties denial of the reckoning to neglect of the orphan and the destitute, in the same order.
Names the failure to honour the orphan and to urge feeding the poor as the actual charge.
Gives two reasons for a man's ruin: he did not believe, and he did not urge feeding the destitute.

studies.applyIt: Feed one person this week who cannot reciprocate and will not thank you where anybody can hear. A meal left somewhere, money given where it cannot be traced back to you. The second item on this list is the concrete one, and it is the only item you can act on before the day is out.

studies.title: Like Donkeys Bolting From A Lion
studies.meaning: The confession closes on a word that ordinarily means certainty, used here as a name for death, the point past which no argument is available. Then the passage turns from them to the audience present, with a question that is not really asking anything. The simile answering it is startling and faintly comic: wild donkeys bolting. Commentators observe that the flight is not from the reminder's content but from its approach, since an animal in flight has evaluated nothing at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The surah addresses people who left gatherings when the recitation began and who took other routes through the town to avoid hearing it. The classical reports describe Meccans stopping their ears and warning visitors away. The comparison reaches out of the town and into the desert, placing a familiar animal behaviour in front of an audience who had all watched it happen.

keyTerms.note: The word for certain knowledge, standing here as a name for death. It is a striking substitution: the one event nobody in the argument disputed becomes the noun for the thing itself.
The second word is an intensive form of taking fright and scattering. Wild asses were known for exactly this, grazing quietly and then bolting at nothing, and the phrase occurs once in the Quran.
Commentators divide between a lion and a band of hunters, and the early lexicographers record both without deciding. The word occurs once in the Quran, which is why the question was never closed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wild asses lived on the margins of the settled land and were hunted for their meat. Poets used them constantly, and the stock scene is a herd standing at a waterhole that explodes into flight at a sound nobody else heard. Anybody who had ridden any distance out of Mecca had watched this happen. The comparison would have raised a laugh before it landed, which is part of how it does its work.
studies.didYouKnow: Both halves of the closing image occur once each in the Quran. The word for the startled herd appears nowhere else, and the word for whatever they are fleeing is rare enough that the early lexicographers could not agree whether it names a lion or a party of hunters. The picture is vivid, and its second half has never been fixed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage diagnoses avoidance rather than disagreement. These people are not shown arguing; they are shown leaving. Making the image an animal one removes reasoning from the account altogether, which is a serious charge: the response is a reflex, below the level at which anything gets weighed. The line just before has already taken away the fallback, saying no intercession reaches them, so flight is the only move left.

crossReferences.why: Describes people putting fingers in their ears and pulling their clothes over themselves to avoid hearing.
Records the instruction to drown the recitation in noise so that nobody can follow it.
Describes hearts shrinking in aversion the moment God alone is mentioned.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you reach for when a particular subject comes up: the phone, a joke, a change of topic. Everybody has one. Name yours this week, and the next time that subject arrives, stay for thirty seconds longer than usual. This passage is not about people who considered something and declined it. It is about people who never got that far.

studies.title: Scrolls Delivered Already Open
studies.meaning: A demand is quoted and then refused, and the refusal names the real obstacle. They want personal documents, each man his own sheet delivered unrolled, and the reply is that evidence was never the problem. The surah then closes with two statements set beside each other and left in tension: whoever wills remembers, and they will not remember unless God wills. Commentators have written at length on the pairing, and the classical position holds both rather than dissolving either into the other.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The reports describe Meccans asking for letters from heaven addressed to them by name, guaranteeing what they were being told, and the surrounding surahs record similar requests for a visible sign. These five ayat close one of the earliest chapters of the Quran, and its last words name God by two descriptions rather than by an act.

keyTerms.note: The second word is an intensive of unrolling. They are asking not for a message but for a document already unfurled, delivered ready to read, with even the act of opening it done for them.
A particle of rebuttal. The Quran uses it to stop a line of thought rather than to refute it, cutting across what has just been said instead of engaging with it on its own terms.
The construction names God as the one to whom that guarding awareness is properly owed, and the phrase immediately after it names Him, in the same form, as the one with whom forgiveness belongs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Written documents existed and carried authority precisely because they were rare. A debt, a treaty or a grant of protection could be committed to writing and kept, and a sealed sheet settled disputes that testimony could not. Asking for a personal scroll was therefore asking for the form of proof their own commerce ran on. The demand was not absurd in that world. It was how a careful man secured anything at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The indefinite word for scrolls occurs twice in the Quran. Here, in a demand for sheets delivered open to each man personally. And in another surah, describing a messenger from God reciting purified scrolls aloud. They asked to be handed pages; the other passage shows pages being read to them, which is what they already had.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal of the documents is the sharpest claim in the passage. More evidence would not move somebody whose obstacle is not evidential, and the ayah says so by naming the absent fear instead of arguing. Then the two closing statements about willing are left side by side without resolution, and the final words of the surah are not about power at all. They are two qualities: that God is rightly heeded, and that forgiveness belongs with Him.

crossReferences.why: Records a demand for a book that can be read, inside a list of signs asked for.
Says a written book sent down on parchment would still be called plain magic.
Ends another early surah on the same pairing of human willing and God's willing.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what evidence would actually change your mind about something you have been avoiding. Not about God: about a habit, a relationship, a decision you keep deferring. Then ask whether that evidence has already arrived. This passage says the people demanding documents had everything they needed and were missing something else entirely.
